title: Designing error contracts
prompt_md: An error contract is a promise about what a function raises and what those exceptions mean. Work through the choices that make a contract usable, and the reading skills that let you honour it under a traceback.

questions.stem_md: Match each failure to the exception a caller would expect it to raise.

left.md: A function is passed a `sort="sideways"` it does not support
A function is passed a string where it needs a list
A requested config key is absent
A withdrawal exceeds the account balance (a domain rule)

questions.explanation_md: Right type, wrong value → `ValueError`; wrong type entirely → `TypeError`; missing key → `KeyError`. Domain rules deserve a *named* exception so callers can catch exactly that condition without catching unrelated errors: `except InsufficientFunds` is a contract; `except Exception` is a shrug.

questions.stem_md: A repository catches a low-level `KeyError` and re-raises a domain `UserNotFound`. Which form preserves the original cause for debugging?

options.md: `raise UserNotFound(uid)` inside the `except` (implicit context is enough).

questions.explanation_md: `raise ... from exc` sets `__cause__`, so the traceback shows "The above exception was the direct cause of the following" and keeps the original `KeyError` visible. Option (b) still chains implicitly (`__context__`) but reads as an accident; (d) *suppresses* the cause with `from None`, which is right only when the underlying error is noise. Translating errors at a boundary is good; hiding the cause while doing so is not.

questions.stem_md: Which of these make an error contract *stronger* (more useful to callers)?

options.md: Wrapping only the single statement that can fail in `try`, not the whole function body.
Catching `Exception` at the top of every function to be safe.
Documenting which exceptions the function raises and when.
Letting exceptions you cannot handle propagate rather than swallowing them.
Raising a specific subclass rather than bare `Exception`.

questions.explanation_md: A narrow `try` avoids catching failures from unrelated lines; documenting and using specific types tells callers what to expect and catch; letting the unhandleable propagate keeps failures loud. Catching `Exception` everywhere is the opposite of a contract: it converts every distinct failure into the same swallowed nothing, and hides bugs that should have surfaced.

questions.stem_md:
```python
def f():
    try:
        return "try"
    finally:
        return "finally"
```
What does `f()` return?

options.md: `"finally"`: a `return` in `finally` replaces the one in `try` and swallows exceptions too.

questions.explanation_md: `finally` always runs, and a `return` (or `break`) inside it overrides whatever the `try` was about to return, and worse, silently discards any in-flight exception. That is why `finally` should be reserved for cleanup and never contain a `return`. Reading this correctly under a traceback saves hours: the function "can't fail" because `finally` ate the error.

questions.stem_md: Two ways to read a possibly-missing dict key. Which is the idiomatic (EAFP) form, and what is its concurrency advantage?

options.md: `try: v = d[k]` / `except KeyError: ...`, no gap between the check and the use, so a concurrent delete cannot slip between them.
`if k in d: v = d[k]`, checking first is always safer.
They are identical in every respect.

questions.explanation_md: EAFP ("easier to ask forgiveness than permission") is idiomatic Python and avoids the time-of-check/time-of-use race in LBYL: with `if k in d` then `d[k]`, another thread (or a callback) can delete `k` in the gap, so the "safe" check does not make the access safe. The `try` form performs the lookup once. (`d.get(k, default)` is the even shorter form when a default will do.)

hints.md: An error contract answers, for the caller: which exceptions can this raise, and what does each mean? Specific types and named domain exceptions make the contract precise; `except Exception` erases it.

Recurring principles: match the built-in type to the failure (value vs type vs lookup); translate at boundaries with `raise ... from` to keep the cause; keep `try` narrow and `finally` for cleanup only; and prefer EAFP to close the check/use race.

Answers: (1) ValueError / TypeError / KeyError / custom, in order. (2) `raise UserNotFound(uid) from exc`. (3) narrow `try`, documenting, letting the unhandleable propagate, and specific subclasses. (4) `"finally"`: it overrides and swallows. (5) the `try/except KeyError` form, which avoids the time-of-check/time-of-use race.
